newsitem.title: USA: Confused dollar backtracks in U.S. on Buba retort.
newsitem.headline: Confused dollar backtracks in U.S. on Buba retort.

text.p: The dollar struggled to find direction against the mark -- first spiking higher then slowly shedding its gains -- as conflicting opinions washed over the currency market in the wake of a statement by Germany's central bank criticizing Bonn's plans to revalue its assets.

The dollar initially jumped to a U.S. high of 1.7047 marks from around 1.69 in relief that the Bundesbank did not flatly refuse to cooperate with the revaluation plan and that no threats of resignation from bank members accompanied the statement -- a rumor that had swirled through the market minutes before the statement's release.

"People initially bought dollars on the fact that the Bundesbank is essentially powerless to stop (European economic and monetary union)," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland in New York.
The unravelling of plans for a single European currency, the euro, would aid the mark which has been dampened by fears it will essentially be replaced in 1999 by a weaker euro.
The plan to revalue Bundesbank gold at near-current levels would help mend holes in Bonn's public finances and aid Germany in meeting the fiscal criteria mandated for membership into EMU.
But traders here sold marks on worries such "tricky accounting" would set a bad precedent which could open the door for less fiscally-stable nations in the first wave of EMU, thus weakening the euro.

"The perception is (Bundesbank members) weren't very hard on the revaluation technique and therefore the market is taking a little bit of a soft-euro approach so the mark weakened and the dollar got a little firmer," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.

"I think that the trade had expected the Bundesbank to be a little more critical. They criticized the plan but said in principle they believe in asset valuation so they didn't really take the government to task," he added.

Jim Powers, a vice president in foreign exchange sales and advisory at Westdeutsche Landesbank in New York, said the apparent rift between Germany's government and central bank also weighed on the mark.
The German coalition government, shortly after the release of the Bundesbank statement, came out with a counterblast of its own.
Bonn said it would stick to plans to revalue despite the central bank's reservations and that the stability and independence of the Bundesbank will not be affected by the revaluation.
"You are seeing the Bundesbank basically taking on the government, disagreeing and condemning their plan on revaluation -- so the dollar was the benefactor," Powers said.

However, within the next hour, the dollar shed its gains to settle at 1.6960/70 marks by 1500 EDT/1900 GMT in relatively quiet trade as fears spread that the rift between German powers and future accounting issues could delay EMU.
"We fell off the highs as the market decided the Bundesbank statement may be powerless but there may be a delay to EMU here. It brought us back down below 1.70 again," Jury said.

In its statement on Wednesday, the Bundesbank said the Bonn revaluation concept ran the risk of undermining the stability of the euro. Also, the bank charged the plan was out of line with rules planned for changes to central bank accounting after the move to a single currency as it linked the revaluation to an immediate payout of the unrealized profit.
This payout should normally only be made at the time of entry to the single European currency, the statement said.
